question: A cylinder of gas sits on a bench. Which question is meaningful, and which is not?

answers.answer: "How much internal energy does it have?" is meaningful; "how much heat does it contain?" is not.
answers.feedback: Correct. Internal energy is a state function, so the gas has a definite amount of it. Heat is one of the two ways energy crosses the boundary, so it belongs to a process, not to a state. A gas contains energy; it does not contain heat.

answers.answer: Both are meaningful — heat is simply the thermal part of the internal energy.
answers.feedback: There is no way to separate internal energy into a "thermal part" that arrived as heat and a "mechanical part" that arrived as work. Two identical gases in identical states may have been prepared by entirely different mixes of heating and compression.

answers.answer: Neither is meaningful, because both depend on the path taken.
answers.feedback: Internal energy does not depend on the path — that is exactly what makes it a state function, and it is why ΔU comes out the same for every route between two states.

answers.answer: "How much heat does it contain?" is meaningful; "how much internal energy?" is not, because energy has no absolute zero.
answers.feedback: It is true that internal energy is measured from an arbitrary reference, but that affects only the zero point; differences are perfectly well defined. Heat, by contrast, has no state-function status at all, not even up to a constant.

question: A gas is taken from state A to state B along two different quasistatic paths. Which statement is always true?

answers.answer: ΔU is the same on both paths; W_on and Q may each differ, but their sum does not.
answers.feedback: Exactly. The first law ties the two path functions to one state function: whatever work fails to supply, heat must make up. This is the whole content of the module in one sentence.

answers.answer: W_on is the same on both paths, because the endpoints are the same.
answers.feedback: Work is the area under the path in the P-V plane, and different paths between the same endpoints enclose different areas. For the standard example the two-leg route costs about 45% more than the isotherm.

answers.answer: Q is the same on both paths, because the temperature change is the same.
answers.feedback: The temperature change is indeed the same — it is a state function. But heat is not determined by ΔT alone; it also depends on how much work was done along the way.

answers.answer: Both W_on and Q are the same, since the gas cannot tell which route it took.
answers.feedback: The gas indeed cannot tell — which is precisely why its *state* functions are identical. The path functions describe what happened at the boundary, and the boundary very much can tell.

question: Using dU = δQ + δW_on, a gas expands isothermally and reversibly. What are the signs of W_on, Q and ΔU?

answers.feedback: Right. The gas pushes its piston out, so work done on it is negative; its temperature and hence its internal energy are unchanged; so heat must flow in to supply exactly the energy the gas spent on its surroundings.
The signs are inverted. In our convention W_on is positive when work is done ON the gas, i.e. during compression. This is expansion.
That describes an adiabatic expansion, where no heat flows and the gas cools. Here the temperature is held fixed, which requires heat to flow in.
For an ideal gas U depends only on temperature, and the temperature is constant, so ΔU must be exactly zero.

question: Why is heat written δQ rather than dQ?

answers.answer: Because there is no function Q of the state whose difference gives the heat transferred.
answers.feedback: Correct, and the cross-derivative test makes it concrete: for an ideal gas ∂M/∂V ≠ ∂N/∂T for δQ, so no such function exists. Dividing by T repairs the failure and produces the entropy — which is why δQ/T earns a proper d.

answers.answer: Because δ denotes a small quantity while d denotes an infinitesimal one.
answers.feedback: Both symbols denote infinitesimals. The distinction is not about size but about whether the infinitesimal is the differential of some state function.

answers.answer: Because heat is not conserved, unlike energy.
answers.feedback: Non-conservation is not the issue: work is not conserved either, and volume is conserved but perfectly exact. What matters is whether a state function exists.

answers.answer: Because heat can be negative, and d is reserved for positive quantities.
answers.feedback: Exact differentials are routinely negative — dU is negative whenever a system loses energy. Sign has nothing to do with exactness.

question: A piston is slammed down suddenly, compressing a gas. Is the work done on the gas equal to the area under a curve in the P-V plane?

answers.answer: No — during the process the gas has no single pressure, so there is no curve to draw.
answers.feedback: Right. The work is -∫P_ext dV, using the pressure applied at the boundary. Only when the process is quasistatic does P_ext equal the gas's own P, and only then is the area under the P-V curve the work.

answers.answer: Yes — the work is always the area under the curve, since that is the definition.
answers.feedback: The definition is δW_on = -P_ext dV at the boundary. Writing the gas's own P there smuggles in the assumption that the gas is in equilibrium throughout, which a slammed piston violates.

answers.answer: Yes, provided the initial and final states are equilibrium states.
answers.feedback: Well-defined endpoints are not enough. The integral needs a well-defined pressure at every point *along* the way, not just at the ends.

answers.answer: No — because work is only defined for reversible processes.
answers.feedback: Work is perfectly well defined for irreversible processes; it is simply not given by the area under a P-V curve for the gas. Engines would be unanalysable otherwise.

question: One mole of ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally and reversibly from 10.0 L to 20.0 L. Compute the work done ON the gas, in joules. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol K).

answers.feedback: W_on = -nRT ln(V2/V1) = -(1)(8.314)(300) ln 2 = -1729 J. The sign is negative because the gas does work on its surroundings. If you obtained +1729 you are using the other sign convention — which is fine elsewhere, but not in this course.

question: A gas is taken around a closed cycle and returns to its exact starting state. Which is true of one complete cycle?

answers.answer: ΔU = 0, and the net work on the gas equals minus the net heat absorbed.
answers.feedback: Correct — and this is what makes engines possible. The state function returns to its value, so the two path functions must cancel each other rather than vanish individually.

answers.answer: All of ΔU, Q and W_on are zero, since nothing has changed.
answers.feedback: Only the state function must return to its value. If Q and W_on both vanished around every loop, no engine could ever produce net work, and yet they plainly do.

answers.answer: ΔU = 0 and W_on = 0, so Q = 0 as well.
answers.feedback: The net work around a loop is minus the enclosed area, which is zero only for a degenerate loop with no area. A genuine cycle encloses area.

answers.answer: The net work equals the area under the upper curve of the cycle.
answers.feedback: It equals the *enclosed* area — the area under the upper branch minus the area under the lower one, since the return leg contributes with the opposite sign.

question: A gas expands adiabatically and quasistatically. What happens to its temperature?

answers.answer: It falls, because the gas does work on its surroundings with no heat flowing in to replace the energy.
answers.feedback: Correct. Adiabatic means Q = 0, so the first law gives ΔU = W_on < 0 for an expansion. The gas pays for the work out of its own internal energy, and for an ideal gas that energy is the temperature.

answers.answer: It stays constant, because "adiabatic" means no temperature change.
answers.feedback: This confuses adiabatic with isothermal. Adiabatic constrains the *heat* (Q = 0); isothermal constrains the *temperature*. They are different constraints, and for an expanding gas they give opposite answers — which is exactly why the two curves in the P-V plane have different slopes.

answers.answer: It rises, because compression of the surroundings heats the gas.
answers.feedback: The gas is expanding, not being compressed. An adiabatic *compression* does raise the temperature, and that is how a diesel engine ignites its fuel.

answers.answer: It stays constant, because no heat enters or leaves.
answers.feedback: No heat crossing the boundary does not mean no energy crossing it. Work is the other channel, and along an adiabat it is the only one.
